questions.q: What problem does plain TOP have with tied values at the cutoff?
options: It picks one row from the tie somewhat arbitrarily and drops the other(s)
It fails with an error whenever a tie exists
It always returns every tied row automatically
Ties are impossible in SQL Server, so this never happens
questions.explain: TOP 5 returns exactly 5 rows even if row 5 and row 6 are genuinely tied — one gets arbitrarily dropped.

questions.q: What does TOP 5 WITH TIES do differently?
options: Returns the top 5 plus any additional rows tied with the value at row 5, potentially returning more than 5 rows
Returns exactly 5 rows, guaranteed, no exceptions
Returns only the tied rows, excluding the rest of the top 5
Sorts tied rows alphabetically as a tiebreaker automatically
questions.explain: WITH TIES can return more rows than the number specified, if there's a tie at the cutoff position.

questions.q: Why does TOP ... WITH TIES require an ORDER BY clause?
options: A 'tie' only has meaning relative to a defined sort order
It doesn't actually require ORDER BY — that's optional
ORDER BY is required for all TOP queries regardless of WITH TIES
WITH TIES sorts the data itself, making ORDER BY redundant
questions.explain: Without an ORDER BY, there's no defined 'cutoff position' for anything to be tied at — SQL Server errors if you omit it.

questions.q: When is WITH TIES the right choice over plain TOP?
options: When 'top N' represents a genuine ranking or leaderboard where dropping a tied value would misrepresent the data
Always — WITH TIES should replace plain TOP in every query
Only when working with text columns
Never — WITH TIES is deprecated in modern SQL Server
questions.explain: For genuine rankings (like 'top 10 highest-paid employees'), WITH TIES avoids arbitrarily excluding someone who's tied for the cutoff spot.

questions.q: Can a WITH TIES query return more rows than the number specified in TOP?
options: Yes — if multiple rows tie at the cutoff position, all of them are included
No, it always returns exactly the specified number
Only if the WHERE clause is also present
Only when using TOP PERCENT WITH TIES
questions.explain: That's the entire point of WITH TIES — it can exceed the specified row count to include every tied row.
